snapshot.title: Teacher unions suspend two-week strike after meeting with Council of State
snapshot.evidenceText: The teacher unions have suspended their two-week old industrial action after a meeting with the Council of State on Friday. They have therefore directed their members to return to the classrooms from Monday, October 12, 2026. This follows a successful meeting with the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission and the Council of State on Friday. Council of State, Employment Ministry, FWSC meet pre-tertiary teachers over strike The government on Friday stepped up its discussions with the three teacher unions with a view to getting them to call off their nine-day industrial action. The move was to enable them to return to the classrooms on Monday, October 12, 2026, for the resumption of academic activities in first and second cycle institutions. In pursuit of that the unions held separate meetings at the Ministry of Labour, Jobs and Employment, Council of State and Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC). After the meeting with the sector minister at the Ministry of Labour, Jobs and Employment, Emmanuel Kwadwo Agyekum, he told journalists that the discussions had centered on the three issues that made them to declare a strike, reports Graphic Online's Emmanuel Bonney. "I would say that we have had a fantastic discussion with the teacher unions. The issues were to deal with their collective agreement, the other issue had to do with the deprived area allowance and the last one was to deal with promotions," he said. He said promotion was a bit problematic because "we had to come in from the front of the Ghana Education Service (GES) and that of the Controller and Accountant General." He said a team had been put together and for the past one week it had some very good results. "As of yesterday (Thursday), we had about 64,000 [teachers] that have been keyed in and confirmed by controller. "So I think definitely we would have a positive results today from the unions," he said. Education Ministry expresses appreciation to teacher unions for suspending strike Meanwhile the Ministry of Education has expressed appreciation to the three teacher unions, the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT), and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG), for suspending their nationwide strike following constructive negotiations with the Government and the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission. It said the ministry acknowledged the unions’ decision as a positive step towards resolving outstanding concerns through dialogue, mutual understanding, and constructive engagement in the best interest of teachers and learners. "The ministry remains committed to working collaboratively with the unions, the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission, and other relevant stakeholders to address outstanding issues and promote teachers’ welfare, while ensuring stability and continuity in the delivery of quality education. "The Ministry appreciates the patience and resilience of teachers, parents, learners, and all stakeholders affected by the industrial action. We urge all parties to sustain the spirit of cooperation and good faith to ensure that the gains made through negotiations are consolidated," it said. The Ministry reaffirmrd its commitment to strengthening industrial harmony and creating an enabling environment in which teachers are valued, supported, and empowered to contribute meaningfully to Ghana’s education transformation agenda.

snapshot.title: NCPTA welcomes end of teachers’ strike, urges compliance | Ghana News Agency
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Kadjebi (O/R), Oct. 10, GNA – The National Council of Parent-Teacher Associations (NCPTA)-Ghana has welcomed the decision by teacher unions to call off their strike. The Council urged all parties to honour the timelines agreed upon to address outstanding concerns. The Council said the resumption of classroom activities would restore teaching and learning, protect the academic calendar and ease the burden on parents and guardians. The strike was called off following a communiqué signed on October 09, 2026, by the government, represented by the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC) and the Ghana Education Service (GES), and teacher unions, including the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG). In a press statement dated October 10 and signed by Mr Gapson Kofi Raphael, the General Secretary of NCPTA-Ghana, the Council expressed gratitude to President John Dramani Mahama and other stakeholders for their roles in resolving the impasse. It also commended the leadership and members of the teacher unions for returning to negotiations and agreeing to resume classroom work. The statement said the agreement outlined timelines for addressing key concerns, including the payment of salary arrears to 51,000 teachers by October 16, 2026, with the remaining payments expected by the end of October. It said modalities for the Deprived Area Allowance were expected to be addressed in January 2027, while the Digital Support Allowance and Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Allowance were scheduled for November and December 2026, respectively. The Council urged the FWSC, GES and teacher unions to work proactively to meet the agreed deadlines, particularly those concerning the expired Collective Agreement and the 20 per cent Deprived Area Allowance. It stressed the need for sustained dialogue and accountability to ensure that the commitments made during negotiations were fulfilled. The statement said the reopening of schools would benefit not only learners but also parents, businesses and the wider economy. It noted that the prolonged closure of schools had placed additional responsibilities on parents, many of whom had to supervise their children at home while working to provide for their families. It added that the disruption had affected school-related businesses, including food vendors, stationery shops, school transport operators, uniform suppliers and caterers under the Ghana School Feeding Programme. The Council said the return to school would help restore learning routines, improve preparations for the Basic Education Certificate Examination (BECE) and the West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE), and ensure continuity in government education programmes. It therefore urged parents and guardians of learners in public basic and secondary schools to prepare their wards for the resumption of classes. The Council also called on school-based PTA executives to collaborate with school management to develop strategies to recover the lost instructional hours. It reaffirmed the importance of cooperation among government, teachers, parents and other stakeholders in safeguarding the quality of pre-tertiary education in Ghana. Schools are expected to resume academic work on Monday is October 12, 2026. The three teacher unions – the Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT), the National Association of Graduate Teachers (NAGRAT) and the Pre-Tertiary Teachers Association of Ghana (PRETAG) – declared the industrial action on September 25, 2026. The unions are demanding payment of salary arrears for teachers who were promoted but had not received the corresponding salaries, payment of the 20 per cent Deprived-Area teacher Allowance and the renewal of their Collective Agreement. snapshot.title: GNAT directs teachers to resume work Monday after strike suspension - Adomonline.com
snapshot.evidenceText: The Ghana National Association of Teachers (GNAT) has suspended its nationwide strike following a series of engagements with government and other stakeholders, including the Council of State. The Association has directed its members to resume normal duties on Monday, October 12, 2026, pending the fulfilment of commitments made during the negotiations. In a statement, GNAT said more than 51,000 members who had been promoted would be placed on their appropriate salary scales, with full payment of arrears and their October salaries, by October 16, 2026. It said the necessary inputs had been made and were awaiting validation. On the ongoing negotiations for a collective agreement, GNAT disclosed that the parties had agreed to increase the Cost of Professional Allowance (CPA) to GH¢3,100, tax-free, with payment expected in December 2026. The Complimentary Digital Support Allowance has also been increased to GH¢1,100, tax-free, and is expected to be paid by the end of November 2026. The Association said negotiations on the collective agreement remained inconclusive, adding that a procedural document outlining how teachers could access the benefits would be finalised with the Ghana Education Service (GES) once the agreement document was completed. GNAT further stated that an agreement had been reached in principle for budgetary provision to be made for the Deprived Area Allowance in the 2027 national budget, with payments expected to begin in January 2027. According to the statement, payments would initially cover teachers serving in island communities and hinterlands, with coverage expected to expand over time. The Association thanked its officers, executives, council members, staff and members for their solidarity and support throughout the industrial action. It assured members of its continued commitment to addressing outstanding concerns and improving conditions within the teaching profession. snapshot.title: Drone strike by Sudan paramilitary kills 41 near Ethiopian border, rights group says
snapshot.evidenceText: A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said. The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said. The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children. The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes. It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help. The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south. Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks. Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm". representative.title: TASIS denies Abu Shandi strike, alleges Egyptian drone attack - The Sudan Times
representative.author: Bobby

snapshot.title: TASIS denies Abu Shandi strike, alleges Egyptian drone attack - The Sudan Times
snapshot.evidenceText: The Sudan Founding Alliance (TASIS) has denied responsibility for the deadly drone strike in Abu Shandi in Sudan’s Blue Nile region, alleging instead that an Egyptian military drone launched from an army-held area carried out the attack. The death toll from Friday’s strike near a displacement site in Abu Shandi, Wad al-Mahi locality, has risen to 41, according to Emergency Lawyers. The group blamed the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a leading member of the TASIS alliance, and said eight children and numerous women were among those killed. TASIS rejected the accusation in a statement issued by its spokesman Ahmed Tugud Lisan, describing reports blaming its forces as an attempt to discredit the alliance following recent military advances in Blue Nile. The alliance alleged that the drone which struck civilians in Abu Shandi belonged to Egypt and had been launched from the police headquarters in Wad al-Mahi by Egyptian technicians. TASIS further alleged that a local figure identified as Mek Zaidan, whom it accused of working with the army-aligned Port Sudan authorities, travelled toward the traditional gold-mining area as the drone approached and withdrew shortly before the strike. The alliance claimed his movements demonstrated prior knowledge of the attack. TASIS said the accusations against its forces were intended to turn local communities against the alliance and encourage recruitment into Sudan’s military and allied Popular Resistance formations. The United Nations has condemned the attack but has not publicly attributed responsibility. UN officials initially reported that around 40 civilians had been killed, most of them women and children, after what the organisation described as a suspected drone strike near a displacement site close to the Sudan-Ethiopia border. The UN called for those responsible to be held accountable under international humanitarian law. The attack occurred amid intensified fighting in Blue Nile between Sudan’s military and the TASIS-aligned forces, including the RSF and Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North. Abu Shandi lies in Wad al-Mahi, an increasingly contested area near the Ethiopian border where thousands of civilians have been displaced by the recent fighting.

snapshot.title: Rights group says paramilitary drone strike in Sudan killed 41 near Ethiopian border – WTOP News
snapshot.evidenceText: CAIRO (AP) — A drone strike blamed on Sudan’s notorious paramilitaries hit a gathering of displaced people on the border with Ethiopia and killed 41, a rights group said. Friday’s strike by the Rapid Support Forces took place in the Abu Shandi area in Sudan’s Blue Nile province, according to Emergency Lawyers, which tracks the war in the northeastern African nation. Among the dead were eight children and many women, the group said. A spokesperson for the RSF didn’t respond to a request for comment. The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said it was appalled by the reported strike that also wounded dozens. “Condemning these senseless killings is essential, but there must also be accountability for this flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law,” said Denise Brown, the U.N. resident and humanitarian coordinator in Sudan in a statement. “As each day goes by in this war, the world continues to accept the suffering of the people of Sudan.” Sudan’s war started in April 2023 when tensions between the military and the RSF exploded into open fighting in the capital, Khartoum, and spread across the country. The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED, though aid groups say the real number is likely higher. It has forced more than 12.4 million to flee their homes, according to U.N. figures, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis. Across Sudan , 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need aid this year, and an estimated 825,000 children face severe acute malnutrition. snapshot.title: Dengue death toll nears 300 as 4 die, 1,631 hospitalised in 24 hours
snapshot.evidenceText: Four people died of dengue and 1,631 were admitted to hospitals across the country in the 24 hours until 8am today (10 October). The latest deaths have taken the country's dengue death toll to 299 this year, according to a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Of the four deaths, one each was reported in Dhaka North City Corporation, Barishal, Chattogram and Khulna division. September recorded the highest monthly dengue death toll so far this year, with 148 deaths. Dengue claimed five lives in total from January to May, followed by 13 deaths in June, 36 in July and 43 in August. Meanwhile, 1,627 dengue patients were discharged from hospitals in the 24 hours, taking the total number of recoveries this year to 91,007. The cumulative number of dengue cases reported across the country has reached 97,082, according to the DGHS. snapshot.title: Major earthquake hits Panama, injures at least 27
snapshot.evidenceText: A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least 27 people, with no deaths reported. The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System. The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that there were no reports of fatalities so far. In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. "Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking." A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles traveled across it. "We are facing a major disaster," President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had "completely collapsed." "It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school," Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, told AFP. There were 27 people with minor injuries across the country as a result of the quake, according to a statement from the National Civil Protection System. The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 12:56 pm local time (1756 GMT) with an epicenter 10 kilometers (six miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province. The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7. A tsunami warning was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist," at the Panamanian government's request. The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating "as normal." Mulino traveled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos. He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off. "We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," Boyd said. Panama City's international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed. Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority. The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers of aid. Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power. His neighbor, David Castillo, told AFP that residents were choosing not to return home because they are "afraid it will happen again." Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province that collapsed. A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed. More than 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute. "What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder," he wrote on X, adding that he had called for a report on the damage. The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide. The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System. The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that there were no reports of fatalities so far. In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. "Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking." A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Another showed a bridge over the Panama Canal shaking violently but remaining upright as vehicles traveled across it. "We are facing a major disaster," President Jose Raul Mulino said, adding that some roads had "completely collapsed." "It was horrible, like nothing we ever experienced. My daughter was trapped in school," Juana Alveo, a 38-year-old cashier at a store in the city of Penonome in central Cocle province, told AFP. There were 27 people with minor injuries across the country as a result of the quake, according to a statement from the National Civil Protection System. The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 12:56 pm local time (1756 GMT) with an epicenter 10 kilometers (six miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in central Herrera province. The USGS initially estimated it to be a magnitude-8.0 quake before revising it down to 7.7. A tsunami warning was issued for the eastern Pacific but later lifted. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist," at the Panamanian government's request. The Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the channel, which connects the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, was unaffected and operating "as normal." Mulino traveled to Penonome to coordinate the disaster response. Health Minister Fernando Boyd said the most affected areas were the provinces of Herrera and Cocle as well as Los Santos. He said the town of Tonosi in Los Santos was completely cut off. "We are trying to figure out how to get there by air, because it's impossible by land," Boyd said. Panama City's international airport, a major hub for the region, was temporarily closed. Several flights were diverted to other airports as a precaution, according to the Civil Aeronautics Authority. The leaders of Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala all sent messages of solidarity and offers of aid. Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power. His neighbor, David Castillo, told AFP that residents were choosing not to return home because they are "afraid it will happen again." Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica. Former president Ricardo Martinelli posted pictures on Instagram of his house in the town of Sona in Veraguas province that collapsed. A church and a hotel in Penonome also suffered extensive damage, images shared on local media showed. More than 80 aftershocks, one above magnitude 6.0, were recorded by the local geosciences institute. "What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder," he wrote on X, adding that he had called for a report on the damage. The education ministry announced the suspension of classes in schools nationwide. The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August. snapshot.title: The Weekly Review, October 5 to 9, 2026 - Statistics Canada
snapshot.evidenceText: Employment declined by 68,000 (-0.3%) in September, split between full-time work (-35,000; -0.2%) and part-time work (-33,000; -0.9%). Employment fell in educational services, health care and social assistance as well as manufacturing. Meanwhile, the employment rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 60.6%. In September, the unemployment rate increased 0.1 percentage points to 6.5%. In August, Canada's merchandise exports rose 2.5%, while imports were down 2.0%. As a result, Canada's merchandise trade surplus with the world widened from $787 million in July to $4.2 billion in August. The total imports decrease during the month was the first decline since January. Despite the decrease, gains were observed in 6 of the 11 product sections. Imports of motor vehicles and parts posted the largest decline in August. Source: Canadian international merchandise trade, August 2026 The operating revenue of the travel arrangement and reservation services industry group rose 8.8% to $18.3 billion in 2025. This follows an increase of 9.3% in 2024. Although operating revenues of these industries posted slower growth in 2025, they still topped the high of $16.8 billion recorded the previous year. In 2025, LGB+ (12%) and gender diverse (15%) people were over three times as likely to have experienced violent victimization (i.e., physical or sexual assault) in the previous 12 months compared with their heterosexual (3.6%) and cisgender (4.1%) counterparts. In addition, approximately half of LGB+ people had been sexually (49%) or physically (52%) assaulted since age 15, higher than their heterosexual counterparts (21% had been sexually assaulted and 31% had been physically assaulted). Source: Violent victimization and unwanted sexual behaviours experienced by 2SLGBTQ+ people in Canada, 2025 Critical mineral production contributed $26.3 billion to the total Canadian economy in 2024, representing roughly a 0.9% share, as measured by nominal gross domestic product (GDP). Measured by real GDP, critical mineral production, grew by 8.2% in 2024. Every aggregation of critical minerals experienced real GDP growth, with the most notable increases coming from platinum group metals (+16.7%) and unrefined prioritized critical minerals (+13.9%; including cobalt, copper and nickel). Source: Economic contribution of critical mineral production in Canada, 2024 The legacy of Terry Fox lives on, long after his death in 1981. Countless Canadians have taken part in the Terry Fox Run every year in September to raise awareness and funds for cancer research. Just over two in five people in Canada will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime , according to estimates based on data from the Canadian Cancer Registry. Cancer has been the leading cause of death in Canada since 2006 . Predicted five-year net survival rates for those diagnosed from 2019 to 2021 were highest for thyroid (97%) and testicular (96%) cancers. representative.title: Canada loses all 2026 job gains. These sectors were hardest hit
representative.author: Reuters Staff

snapshot.title: Canada’s 2026 job gains have been erased. The hardest-hit area wasn’t the one facing U.S. tariffs
snapshot.evidenceText: OTTAWA — Canada’s economy shed a net 68,300 jobs in September and the unemployment rate edged up, data showed on Friday, erasing all the employment gains recorded earlier this year. The unexpected drop follows a decline of 41,700 jobs in August, Statistics Canada said. The unemployment level in September inched up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent in August. September was the first full month after a new round of U.S. tariffs took effect against Canada. However, the largest job losses were in the public sector, particularly health care, social assistance and education, as the government cut international student permits. Analysts polled by Reuters had forecast an increase of 9,200 jobs and an unemployment rate of 6.5 per cent. With September’s decline, Canada has lost a net 41,200 jobs so far this year, compared with a gain of 211,300 in the same period of 2025. Job losses were split almost evenly between full-time and part-time positions. Manufacturing, a sector partly exposed to U.S. tariffs, lost a net 12,700 jobs. Economists have said the latest U.S. tariffs are unlikely to have a major impact on employment data in the coming months. Money markets are no longer pricing in a rate increase from the Bank of Canada this month, although expectations of a 25 basis point hike had edged higher. Markets expect a 25-basis-point increase in December. “Given the recent deterioration in the labour market, Canadian central bankers will likely need to keep rates unchanged later this month,” Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said in a note. “That said, we expect that higher energy prices will begin feeding other categories of inflation this fall, and could force officials to tighten policy soon.” The labour force participation rate, which measures the share of the population either working or looking for work, fell 0.2 percentage points to 64.8 per cent in September, its lowest level in 29 years excluding the pandemic period. The decline was driven largely by an aging population leaving the workforce and slower immigration reducing the number of replacements. Employment among young people aged 15-24 fell by 48,000 in September after a smaller decline in August. Growth in average hourly wages for permanent employees, a closely watched measure of inflation pressures, accelerated to 2.3 per cent year on year in September from two per cent in August, Statistics Canada said. The Canadian dollar weakened after the report, falling 0.44 per cent to $1.4287 per US dollar, or 69.99 US cents. Yields on two-year Canadian government bonds were down 9.5 basis points at 2.410 per cent. --- Reporting by Promit Mukherjee. Editing by Dale Smith and Mark Potter

snapshot.title: Eight firms, one family, Tk 1,200cr ‘embezzled’
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. Three years after the contract was signed, work on a 10.6km road in Bhandaria upazila, Pirojpur, has yet to begin. Yet the contractor has received Tk 13.23 crore, more than 80 percent of the Tk 15.92 crore contract value. The road is one example of the alleged plunder of public money by a clique of government officials, contractors and influential politicians, including two former MPs from the district. The Pirojpur district office of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) investigated 17 projects undertaken between 2020 and 2024 and found corruption and embezzlement worth Tk 1,195 crore in at least eight. All eight projects went to firms owned by members of one family: former Pirojpur-2 independent MP Mohiuddin Maharaj, his three brothers and a sister-in-law. Documents show premature payments, duplicate payments for the same work, substandard materials and poor recordkeeping. Some official records are missing altogether. In one case, a contractor received Tk 996 crore against an approved cost of Tk 936 crore, Tk 60 crore more than the contract value, according to an LGED monitoring report from August 2026. The Southern Country Iron Bridge Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Project, aimed at improving connectivity in 42 upazilas in Barishal, was due for completion in June 2026. Only half the work has been completed. The Daily Star’s analysis of the eight projects shows that their combined contract value was Tk 2,141 crore. Based on the work completed, only Tk 826.38 crore should have been disbursed. Instead, Tk 2,069 crore was released -- about Tk 1,243 crore more than warranted. In August, The Daily Star visited the proposed Maliar Haat-Koikhali Haat road in Bhandaria and found parts of the route in particularly poor condition. Montu Hawlader, a motorcyclist who regularly uses the road, said, “I fell off my motorcycle six times in recent months. I escaped injury each time only because there was no traffic.” The road is part of the 179-package Barishal Division Important Upazila and Union Road Widening and Strengthening Project. Overall progress stands at just 15 percent. Yet. Tk 624 crore -- 89 percent of the contract value -- has already been disbursed, documents show. The road contract went to EFTE. ETCL (Pvt.) Limited, run by managing director Merajul Islam, former Sadar upazila chairman and Mohiuddin’s brother. Merajul owns four of the eight firms: EFTE. ETCL, EFTE Enterprise, EFTE Trading Corporation Limited and South Bangla Trading Limited. His wife, Shamima Akhter, owns a fifth, Shimu Enterprise. The sixth, Horinpala Trade International, belongs to Mohiuddin himself. The remaining two firms belong to Mohiuddin’s younger brothers: M/S Teli Khali Construction, owned by Md Shamsuddin, and Ishan Enterprises, owned by Mohammad Salahuddin, according to the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). Teli Khali and EFTE. ETCL together won nearly 375 contracts worth more than Tk 1,000 crore from the Pirojpur LGED executive engineer’s office. They were the single bidders in nearly 200 cases, meaning no one competed except them, or others were not even allowed to compete, said Mohammad Tauhidul Islam, who studies public procurement at Transparency International Bangladesh. “The way the money was siphoned off is unbelievable,” a top LGED official told The Daily Star, requesting anonymity. The scale of the corruption, the official said, points to the involvement of senior government officials, the ministry and local offices. An LGED investigation report from January 2025 reached a similar conclusion. It said the irregularities and embezzlement “was not possible without the direct support of politically influential figures at the local and national levels and the highest-ranking officials at the policy level of the previous [Awami League] government.” Besides Mohiuddin and Merajul, the report names SM Rezaul Karim, former Pirojpur-1 Awami League MP and minister; Nure Alam Shahin, Rezaul’s brother and former Nazirpur upazila chairman; and Md Tofazzel Hossain Miah, former principal secretary at the Prime Minister’s Office. AKM Mozammel Hoque Khan, accounts officer at LGED’s Pirojpur office, also told investigators that firms, politicians and officials had colluded. He specifically named former executive engineer Abdus Sattar Howlader, who approved the bills. Current Executive Engineer Md Azizur Rahman said all eight contractors had been blacklisted and their projects would be cancelled once the chief engineer approved the move. The office had received no instructions from headquarters on resuming the work. A top LGED official said work on projects tainted by corruption allegations and legal proceedings would likely remain stalled until the legal processes ended. “So it will take considerable time before the work can resume,” he said. LGED investigators and a recent audit also found serious irregularities in project records. In 2025, the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General raised audit objections worth Tk 2,666 crore across the 17 projects. Among the anomalies were bridges built without approach roads and bills submitted for the same work under multiple projects. Under the Supporting Rural Bridges Programme, a contract worth Tk 21.42 lakh was signed with EFTE. ETCL. Yet, a cheque for Tk 15.04 crore was issued to Rupali Construction instead. Officials at the District Accounts and Finance Officer’s Office could not produce the bills, vouchers or other documents to explain the payment. Several files contained only note sheets signed by the accountant and the executive engineer. At least 340 documents were missing from the accounts section. Mozammel told the LGED investigation team in December 2024 that the documents had been kept by contractors on the executive engineers’ instructions. He also said Abdus Sattar Howlader had asked him to sign irregular bills. “Just sign it. You will not face any consequences; I will bear full responsibility,” Mozammel quoted Howlader as saying. In 2025, the ACC filed eight cases against 27 people, including Mohiuddin, his three brothers, Merajul’s wife and 22 officials of the local LGED and the District Accounts Office. The cases concern the withdrawal of Tk 1,080 crore from schemes under the eight projects despite only partial completion of the work. The ACC says the money was mainly drawn through the eight firms registered in the names of Mohiuddin and his relatives. Six officials were arrested. Mozammel died in jail, while five other District Accounts Office officials are out on bail. The remaining accused are fugitives, said Md Aminul Islam, deputy director at the ACC’s Pirojpur office. In March 2026, the ACC filed nine more cases against Mohiuddin, Howlader and their families over assets allegedly acquired beyond their known sources of income. The cases are under investigation. The ACC has also seized assets worth about Tk 300 crore belonging to the accused in Pirojpur and Dhaka, Aminul said. Contacted by phone, Rezaul said he was neither a minister nor a contractor during the period and had no authority over LGED. However, records show he became fisheries and livestock minister in a February 2020 reshuffle, after previously serving as housing and public works minister. Shahin, elected chairman in 2024, denied that either he or his brother Rezaul was involved in the embezzlement. Mohiuddin said he was elected an independent MP only in January 2024, served for seven months and held no significant position. Merajul denied all allegations, saying many projects reported as incomplete had actually been completed. He acknowledged some excess payments made to prevent allocated funds from lapsing at the end of the fiscal year, but insisted that no money had been withdrawn without work. He said he still wanted to complete the projects and was willing to adjust any excess payments. Tofazzel and Howlader’s phones were switched off. snapshot.title: Canadian economy lost 68,000 jobs in September, marking second straight month of surprise declines | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September, according to Statistics Canada, marking a second straight month of losses. The unemployment rate ticked up by 0.1 percentage points to 6.5 per cent, which is where it stood at the start of 2026. The figures bucked economists' predictions for a gain of 9,200 positions in September. It comes after another surprise last month of 42,000 job losses for August , which snapped a hot streak for the labour market. Before the two monthly declines, Statistics Canada data showed employment trending upward, with 181,000 jobs added between April and July. Employment is still up compared to a year ago by 95,000 positions. BMO chief economist Doug Porter said job figures are often volatile, and have been especially so in recent years. Still, he noted it's rare to see two months in a row of job losses of this size. "There's no question, this is a disappointing result," Porter said. "It does suggest the economy was struggling in the early fall." By sector, educational services, health care and social assistance, and manufacturing led the declines. More workers in "other services," which includes things like repair and maintenance, offset the losses. Porter says the drop in education jobs, which was concentrated in Quebec, could be a bit of a blip, but says it could also point to weakness in the sector with fewer international students studying in the country. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham adds that while some data volatility is likely behind the poor report, losses in manufacturing could be a sign that new tariffs, which came into effect in August, are taking a toll. Statistics Canada says job losses were split between full- and part-time work and were concentrated in the public sector, which dropped 70,000 roles in the month. The number of public sector employees is down by 119,000 compared to the same time last year. The private sector added some jobs and held steady however — a silver lining, according to Porter. Deloitte Canada cuts GDP growth forecast by 20% as tariffs grip economy amid Trump's trade war The decline was concentrated in youth aged 15 to 24, who accounted for 48,000 job losses, according to the data agency. But the pool of young workers also shrank in September, leaving the unemployment rate for that group relatively unchanged at 13 per cent. Core-aged women, between 25 and 54 years old, also held 28,000 fewer positions, and the number of women in that age group looking for work increased. Quebec led the job losses by province, with 49,000 jobs lost in the month, while B.C. followed with 20,000 fewer jobs. Alberta, on the other hand, added 23,000 positions. snapshot.title: Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the Peace Prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim. Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world. At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity. And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence. In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form. Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.

snapshot.title: Navi Pillay, former UN human rights chief, wins Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said. Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza. Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes. "Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said. "At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity." Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'". Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom" . Pillay dedicated her award to "all the survivors of international crimes" and the practitioners of international justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign". Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban. She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court. Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president. She was elected to the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2003. From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law. The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements. The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies". The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes. Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice". It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes." US President Donald Trump, who has previously expressed a desire to receive the prize, reposted a statement on social media that said the Nobel committee had "demeaned" the award by giving it to someone it described as an "unabashed hater of America and Israel". The US later announced sweeping sanctions on the court , saying it wanted to restrict its resources and ability to operate. The ICC called the move an assault on the rule of law. Nobel committee chair Frydnes said the organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide by handing Pillay the peace prize. Asked about Pillay's UN commission on the matter, he replied her award had been given "for her whole work". Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people. Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated" . UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity". Meanwhile, UN Secretary General António Guterres said she had been "a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time". South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally". Amnesty International secretary general Agnès Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award. "At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said. snapshot.title: Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 - Nobel Peace Prize
snapshot.evidenceText: The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 goes to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order. This year’s laureate has been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The Norwegian Nobel Committee has decided to award the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. The first Nobel Peace Prize was awarded 125 years ago. Already then, the Norwegian Nobel Committee underscored the importance of resolving conflicts through international law – a theme that has remained prominent throughout the history of the Peace Prize. The reach of international law expanded after the Second World War, in particular with the creation of the UN institutions. The key insight was that lasting peace must be built on legal principles, not on the will of the strong or a fragile balance of power. Additional legal mechanisms were introduced in the post-war decades, and momentum picked up further after the end of the Cold War However, the rules-based international order has never been perfect. The greatest powers have often evaded responsibility. In practice, cases brought under international law have produced different results depending on who is the perpetrator and who is the victim. Nonetheless, we have seen that more and more conflicts are being addressed through diplomacy, treaties and legal mechanisms, rather than threats, violence and warfare. Leaders and populations alike have come to the same conclusion: international law is a foundation for a more peaceful world. At a time of existential challenges – including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time – international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity. And yet, the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful co-existence. In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law. She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor. In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda The Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 springs directly from Alfred Nobel’s will. Navi Pillay strengthens fraternity between nations and – by systematically advancing the use of tribunals for peace and justice – she provides substance, direction and motivation for peace conferences in their modern form. Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time. Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.

snapshot.evidenceText: People being evacuated from hospital after a severe 7.6 magnitude earthquake hit the country, in Panama City on Oct. 9, 2026. According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), a magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook Panama sparking panic in the capital, though no casualties or damage have been reported so far. PANAMA CITY (AP) — Two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks roiled southern Panama Friday afternoon, collapsing buildings near the epicenter and prompting evacuations across the country. The earlier quake, felt as far away as neighboring Colombia , was centered about 6 miles southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 6 miles. The USGS initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7. (MORE: Hurricane Isaias is closing in on Gulf Coast landfall tonight ) Visibly shaken residents of Panama City, the capital, gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday. “We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.” Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value. Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt. Despite the strength of the successive quakes, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino said authorities had not documented anyone killed as of Friday evening, though he cautioned that could change in the coming hours or days. “Nobody was ready, and no one is ever ready for this type of disaster,” Mulino said, after calling for calm earlier in the day. People check their mobile phones outside the maternity ward of the Santo Tomas hospital, after a 7.6 magnitude earthquake hit the country, in Panama City on Oct. 9, 2026. A severe magnitude 7.6 earthquake shook Panama, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), sparking panic in the capital, though no casualties or damage have been reported so far. Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months. Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela’s La Guaira state in June , killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people . (Live updates: Tornado threat rises as Cat 3 Hurricane Isaias closes in ) The notably lesser toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdés, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos and there were no reports of damages in Panama City. Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, around 93 miles from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways. Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday afternoon that it was reopening. The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage. The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region. Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates. Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 25,000-mile arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur. The National Weather Service lifted a tsunami warning issued shortly after the quakes on Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. Alerts issued by El Salvador and Chile for Easter Island were also lifted. Néstor Luque, director of the Geosciences Institute at the University of Panama, said waves between 3 to 10 feet were expected around Isla Cañas and the southern coast of Los Santos province, but major waves weren't expected beyond that. Seawater had already reached homes near the coast on Isla Cañas, he said. Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region on Friday afternoon. Mulino thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he was closely watching the situation in Panama and “rapidly mobilizing resources and personnel to assist” at the request of Panama's government. “The United States stands with the people of Panama,” Rubio wrote on X. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella , whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.” Acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez, Costa Rican President Laura Fernández Delgado, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Peru's government also offered assistance. “Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” de la Espriella wrote on X. snapshot.title: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake hits Panama | The National
snapshot.evidenceText: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, sparking warnings about tsunamis off the country's coast. The quake had a depth of 12.6km and its epicentre was in Herrera Province, roughly 200km to the south-west of the Panama Canal , according to the US Geological Survey. Some buildings were reported damaged but the critical Panama Canal was not affected, nor was the passage of ships through the trade waterway. Flights were suspended for several hours at Tocumen International Airport, a major regional hub, but had resumed by Friday evening. The USGS initially registered a magnitude of 8.0 for the earthquake before revising it. Panama ’s geological institute reported the quake as a 7.2 magnitude. Local newspaper La Prensa said buildings, businesses, schools and homes in several regions were evacuated following the earthquake. Earthquakes of this magnitude are rare in Panama, and television images ⁠showed elderly residents reduced to tears in the streets as a series of weaker aftershocks ​rattled ⁠the country. “We’re scared. It’s just the ‌two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it ​could fall on us,” Ricardo Brown told Reuters by phone from the Las Minas area of Herrera Province. He said the quake had damaged several other homes. Tremors were felt as far as San Jose, the capital of neighbouring Costa Rica, according to a Reuters witness. Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told local outlet Telemetro Reporta that aftershocks had been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province. Videos shared by La Prensa showed that the tower of a cathedral had collapsed, along with several balconies of a residential ​building in Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and ‌Panama City. In the capital, the ⁠service on two lines of the Panama ​City Metro was temporarily suspended for safety reasons, the operator said. Nationwide, the ministry of education ‌ordered schools to close. Panama had been due to hold a national evacuation drill next Monday ​to test the country's emergency response to earthquakes. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has warned of the potential for tsunami waves off the coast of Panama, as well as the western coasts of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru. The United Arab Emirates expressed its solidarity with the Republic of Panama following the earthquake. In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirmed that the UAE stands alongside the Republic of Panama and its people as they address the aftermath of the earthquake. Friday’s quake was the latest to hit Latin America in recent months. Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes in late June that killed nearly 6,500 people, according to the government’s official toll. The quakes caused widespread destruction, particularly along the country’s northern coast. A powerful earthquake hit Colombia on August 10, levelling buildings and causing major damage in cities including Cali and Pereira. The death toll eventually rose above 330, while the government declared an economic emergency as it confronted a rebuilding bill estimated at roughly $10 billion.

representative.title: Eight firms, one family, Tk 1,200 cr ‘siphoned off’

snapshot.title: Pirojpur LGED Corruption: Tk 1,200cr Public Fund Probe | The Daily Star
snapshot.evidenceText: Eight development projects went to firms owned by one family. Documents show payments far ahead of the work, missing records, and a road that is mostly paid for, though the construction work has not yet begun. Three years after the contract was signed, work on a 10.6km road in Bhandaria upazila, Pirojpur, has yet to begin. Yet the contractor has received Tk 13.23 crore , more than 80 percent of the Tk 15.92 crore contract value. The road is one example of the alleged plunder of public money by a clique of government officials, contractors and influential politicians, including two former MPs from the district. The Pirojpur district office of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) investigated 17 projects undertaken between 2020 and 2024 and found corruption and embezzlement worth Tk 1,195 crore in at least eight. All eight projects went to firms owned by members of one family: former Pirojpur-2 independent MP Mohiuddin Maharaj, his three brothers and a sister-in-law. Documents show premature payments, duplicate payments for the same work, substandard materials and poor recordkeeping. Some official records are missing altogether. Share of each contract’s value: work done, paid beyond the work done Tk crore, all eight projects together: work done, paid beyond it Each bar is one of the eight projects, drawn against its contract value. Grey is the share of the work done, by the LGED’s figures. Red is what was paid on top of that. In all eight projects, the amount paid was higher than the value of the work done. In one case, a contractor received Tk 996 crore against an approved cost of Tk 936 crore, Tk 60 crore more than the contract value, according to an LGED monitoring report from August 2026. The Southern Country Iron Bridge Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Project, aimed at improving connectivity in 42 upazilas in Barishal, was due for completion in June 2026. Only half the work has been completed. The road shown above is part of the 179-package Barishal Division Important Upazila and Union Road Widening and Strengthening Project. Overall progress stands at just 15 percent. Yet, Tk 624 crore — around 90 percent of the contract value — has already been disbursed, documents show. The Daily Star’s analysis of the eight projects shows that their combined contract value was Tk 2,141 crore. Based on the work completed, only Tk 826.38 crore should have been disbursed. Instead, Tk 2,069 crore was released — about Tk 1,243 crore more than warranted. In August, The Daily Star visited the proposed Maliar Haat-Koikhali Haat road in Bhandaria and found parts of the route in particularly poor condition. Montu Hawlader, a motorcyclist who regularly uses the road, said, “I fell off my motorcycle six times in recent months. I escaped injury each time only because there was no traffic.” The contractor of the road in question is EFTE. ETCL (Pvt.) Limited, whose managing director is Merajul Islam, brother of former Pirojpur-2 MP Mohiuddin Maharaj. Including this, he owns four of the firms that won the projects where corruption and embezzlement were found. The three others are EFTE Enterprise, EFTE Trading Corporation Limited and South Bangla Trading Limited. A fifth, Shimu Enterprise, belongs to his wife, Shamima Akhter. The sixth company, Horinpala Trade International, is owned by Mohiuddin Maharaj himself. The remaining two firms belong to Mohiuddin’s younger brothers: M/S Teli Khali Construction, owned by Md Shamsuddin, and Ishan Enterprises, owned by Mohammad Salahuddin, according to the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC). Two of these companies — M/S Teli Khali Construction and EFTE. ETCL (Pvt.) Limited — together secured nearly 375 contracts from the office of the executive engineer of Pirojpur LGED worth more than Tk 1,000 crore. They were the sole bidders in nearly 200 cases, meaning others were not even allowed to compete, said Mohammad Tauhidul Islam, who studies public procurement at Transparency International Bangladesh. “The way the money was siphoned off is unbelievable.” The scale of the corruption, the official said, points to the involvement of senior government officials, the ministry and local offices. An LGED investigation report from January 2025 reached a similar conclusion. It said the irregularities and embezzlement “was not possible without the direct support of politically influential figures at the local and national levels and the highest-ranking officials at the policy level of the previous [Awami League] government.” AKM Mozammel Hoque Khan, accounts officer at LGED’s Pirojpur office, also told investigators that firms, politicians and officials had colluded. He specifically named former executive engineer Abdus Sattar Howlader, who approved the bills. Current Executive Engineer Md Azizur Rahman said all eight contractors had been blacklisted and their projects would be cancelled once the chief engineer approved the move. The office had received no instructions from headquarters on resuming the work. A top LGED official said work on projects tainted by corruption allegations and legal proceedings would likely remain stalled until the legal processes ended. “So it will take considerable time before the work can resume,” he said. LGED investigators and a recent audit also found serious irregularities in project records. In 2025, the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General raised audit objections worth Tk 2,666 crore across the 17 projects. Among the anomalies were bridges built without approach roads and bills submitted for the same work under multiple projects. Under the Supporting Rural Bridges Programme, a contract worth Tk 21.42 lakh was signed with EFTE. ETCL. Yet, a cheque for Tk 15.04 crore was issued to Rupali Construction instead. Tk 15.04 crore Cheque issued to Rupali Construction Contract, Tk 21.42 lakh signed with EFTE. ETCL (Pvt.) Limited Officials at the District Accounts and Finance Officer’s Office could not produce the bills, vouchers or other documents to explain the payment. Several files contained only note sheets signed by the accountant and the executive engineer. Mozammel told the LGED investigation team in December 2024 that the documents had been kept by contractors on the executive engineers’ instructions. He also said Abdus Sattar Howlader had asked him to sign irregular bills. “Just sign it. You will not face any consequences; I will bear full responsibility,” In 2025, the ACC filed eight cases against 27 people, including Mohiuddin, his three brothers, Merajul’s wife and 22 officials of the local LGED and the District Accounts Office. The cases concern the withdrawal of Tk 1,080 crore from schemes under the eight projects despite only partial completion of the work. The ACC says the money was mainly drawn through the eight firms registered in the names of Mohiuddin and his relatives. Six of the accused officials were arrested in connection with the case. Among them, the accounts officer of the LGED Pirojpur office, AKM Mozammel Hoque Khan, died in jail, while five officials from the Accounts Office are out on bail. The rest of the accused are fugitives, said Md Aminul Islam, deputy director at ACC’s Pirojpur district office. snapshot.evidenceText: Eight development projects went to firms owned by one family. Documents show payments far ahead of the work, missing records, and a road that is mostly paid for, though the construction work has not yet begun. Three years after the contract was signed, work on a 10.6km road in Bhandaria upazila, Pirojpur, has yet to begin. Yet the contractor has received Tk 13.23 crore , more than 80 percent of the Tk 15.92 crore contract value. The road is one example of the alleged plunder of public money by a clique of government officials, contractors and influential politicians, including two former MPs from the district. The Pirojpur district office of the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) investigated 17 projects undertaken between 2020 and 2024 and found corruption and embezzlement worth Tk 1,195 crore in at least eight. All eight projects went to firms owned by members of one family: former Pirojpur-2 independent MP Mohiuddin Maharaj, his three brothers and a sister-in-law. Documents show premature payments, duplicate payments for the same work, substandard materials and poor recordkeeping. Some official records are missing altogether. Share of each contract’s value: work done, paid beyond the work done Tk crore, all eight projects together: work done, paid beyond it Each bar is one of the eight projects, drawn against its contract value. Grey is the share of the work done, by the LGED’s figures. Red is what was paid on top of that. In all eight projects, the amount paid was higher than the value of the work done. Limited, whose managing director is Merajul Islam, brother of former Pirojpur-2 MP Mohiuddin Maharaj.
